title: Materials Transformed - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Discover the rules for claiming Materials Transformed during experimental development in our Canadian SR&ED tax credit glossary.
summary: Under Canada's SR&ED program, materials transformed are materials incorporated into an experimental prototype or pilot plant during systematic testing in Canada. Claimants include 100% of the cost in the Section 37 pool and ITC base on Form T661, but if the prototype is later sold or used commercially, the lesser of proceeds and claimed cost is clawed back.

1. Executive Legislative Architecture and Statutory Foundations

Canada's research and development tax incentive framework, formally known as the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, represents the single largest federal source of financial support for industrial innovation, distributing over $4 billion in tax assistance across more than 20,000 claimants annually. The program operates through a dual-mechanism statutory architecture embedded within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945. First, Section 37 of the ITA permits taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to pool current—and, following recent legislative restorations, qualifying capital—SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada, allowing those expenditures to be deducted in full against current-year business income or carried forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. Second, Section 127 of the ITA establishes the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC), which generates either a cash refund or a dollar-for-dollar reduction of federal Part I tax payable based on a statutory percentage of the claimant's "qualified expenditures" as defined under subsection 127(9).

The administration of the SR&ED program is bifurcated between two federal institutions to balance fiscal policy control with technical enforcement. The Department of Finance Canada retains exclusive responsibility for legislative policy, statutory drafting, rate calibration, and fiscal consultations. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the program operationally, exercising statutory authority over technical eligibility reviews, financial expenditure audits, pre-claim advisory services, and notice of assessment issuances.
1.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

The gateway to all federal and harmonized provincial R&D tax incentives is the legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. The statute defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. This overarching requirement is segmented into three primary categories of eligible scientific or technological activity, supplemented by a bounded list of eligible support work and a strict set of statutory exclusions.

Under paragraph 248(1)(a), basic research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, whereas paragraph 248(1)(b) defines applied research as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Across Canadian industry, however, the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims fall under paragraph 248(1)(c), which governs experimental development. Experimental development is defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Commercial enterprises typically rely on paragraph (c) because industrial R&D predominantly seeks to resolve technological uncertainties that impede new product architectures or manufacturing processes rather than pure academic inquiry.

Beyond direct scientific or experimental activities, paragraph 248(1)(d) extends eligibility to eight specific categories of support work: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research, whether automated or otherwise. Crucially, such work qualifies only to the extent that it is commensurate with the needs of, and directly in support of, basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada. Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude a wide array of commercial, routine, and extractive activities from the definition of SR&ED, even when performed by scientific personnel using advanced instrumentation. These statutory exclusions bar claims for market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.

body.text: 2. The 2024–2026 Federal Legislative Modernization Wave

Between 2024 and 2026, the Canadian federal SR&ED regime underwent its most significant structural overhaul since the 2012–2014 austerity reforms, shifting away from narrow private-company restrictions toward broader capitalization support, public company inclusion, and commercialization alignment. This policy pivot emerged from persistent macroeconomic concerns that although Canada offered generous support for early-stage private research, scaling domestic firms faced a steep reduction in tax support upon going public, lacked incentives to invest in physical R&D equipment, and struggled to commercialize and retain intellectual property domestically.
2.1 Department of Finance Consultations and Budget 2024 Commitments

On January 31, 2024, the Department of Finance Canada initiated a comprehensive two-phase public consultation aimed at modernizing the SR&ED program. Phase One ran from January 31, 2024, to April 15, 2024, soliciting stakeholder input on seven structural questions: how to maintain SR&ED effectiveness across business scales; whether to revise the statutory definition of SR&ED and its eligibility criteria; how to optimize complementarity with direct grant programs; how to target assistance more effectively; how to ensure the domestic retention of intellectual property (IP) within Canadian-owned businesses; how to streamline administrative compliance for entrepreneurs; and how to fund enhancements within existing fiscal envelopes.

In Budget 2024: Fairness for Every Generation, tabled on April 16, 2024, the federal government departed from its initial cost-neutral consultation premise and committed $600 million over four years commencing in 2025 (subsequently calibrated at $750 million over five years starting in 2025–26), with $150 million per year on an ongoing basis, to expand SR&ED program support. Budget 2024 concurrently launched Phase Two of the SR&ED consultations, which remained open until May 27, 2024, specifically directing technical design discussions toward extending the enhanced 35% refundable ITC rate to Canadian public corporations and re-evaluating capital expenditure eligibility.
2.2 The 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) Structural Reforms

The legislative outcome of the 2024 consultations crystallized in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), released on December 16, 2024, which proposed three foundational enhancements effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Budget 2025, tabled on November 4, 2025, confirmed and expanded these measures, which were enacted by Bill C-15 upon Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. The first major reform expanded the enhanced 35% expenditure limit and its corresponding corporate size phase-out thresholds. Prior to December 16, 2024, only Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) qualified for the enhanced 35% ITC rate on up to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $3 million, which phased out when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada by the associated corporate group ranged between $10 million and $50 million. For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the 2024 FES proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit on which the 35% rate applies from $3 million to $4.5 million; Budget 2025 raised the proposed limit to $6 million, and Bill C-15 enacted the $6 million limit for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Simultaneously, the taxable capital phase-out thresholds were raised from the legacy $10 million–$50 million corridor to $15 million and $75 million, respectively, preventing growing mid-market technology and manufacturing companies from prematurely losing access to refundable R&D support.

The second pillar of the 2024 FES extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC rate to eligible Canadian public corporations. Historically, when a Canadian technology or life sciences company executed an initial public offering (IPO) on a stock exchange, it lost CCPC status and saw its SR&ED ITC rate drop from a 35% refundable credit to a 15% non-refundable credit, creating a severe working-capital penalty for public market financing. The 2024 FES rectified this structural disincentive by extending the enhanced 35% refundable ITC up to the annual expenditure limit ($6 million as enacted) to eligible Canadian public corporations. To qualify as an eligible Canadian public corporation throughout a taxation year, an entity must satisfy three cumulative statutory tests: it must be resident in Canada; it must have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange, or have validly elected to be a public corporation; and it must not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons. Contrary to CCPCs, whose expenditure limit is tied to taxable capital, eligible Canadian public corporations see their expenditure limit phased out based on average gross revenue over the three preceding taxation years.

The third reform of the 2024 FES, likewise enacted by Bill C-15, provided for the full restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures and equipment lease costs. Reversing the elimination of capital expenditure eligibility that had been in effect since January 1, 2014, the 2024 FES reinstated both the Section 37 income deduction and the Section 127 ITC for SR&ED capital expenditures and equipment lease costs. The restored rules mirror the pre-2014 statutory architecture and apply to depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and, in respect of lease costs, to amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024. Within the expenditure limit, CCPCs and eligible Canadian public corporations earn a 35% ITC that is 100% refundable on current expenditures and 40% refundable on eligible capital expenditures. Above the expenditure limit, the ITC rate reverts to 15%, where qualifying CCPCs whose prior-year income is within the qualifying income limit receive 40% refundability on current and capital spending, whereas eligible Canadian public corporations receive no refundability on expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit.
2.3 Budget 2026 Expansion: Regulatory Validation and Intellectual Property Costs

Building upon the 2024 FES, federal Budget 2026 proposed a major broadening of the SR&ED activity and cost base for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026, backed by an estimated fiscal commitment of $930 million over five years and $235 million per year ongoing. Whereas legacy SR&ED doctrine strictly terminated eligibility the moment technological uncertainty was resolved—thereby excluding post-R&D regulatory certification and patent prosecution—Budget 2026 introduced two interconnected additions to bridge the gap between experimental development and commercial deployment.

First, the Budget 2026 proposal incorporates regulatory and certification testing into the SR&ED regime by adding tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements where carried out for the purpose of obtaining the initial approval or certification necessary to commercialize a product or process developed through an eligible SR&ED project. This reform would directly benefit capital-intensive regulated sectors—including medical devices, pharmaceuticals, natural health and food products, aerospace, automotive components, and electrical equipment requiring safety certification—where products cannot legally enter commercial markets without regulator or certification body sign-off. Claimable expenditures would encompass the standard SR&ED cost categories: wages and salaries, materials, contracting costs, overhead, and machinery and equipment. Conversely, routine compliance renewals, post-market recertifications, and regulatory testing unconnected to an underlying eligible SR&ED project would remain strictly excluded.

Second, Budget 2026 proposes to bring costs reasonably incurred to register and maintain intellectual property (IP) protection within the pool of qualified SR&ED expenditures, provided the underlying IP was developed in the course of an eligible SR&ED project. Four categories of statutory IP would qualify for this treatment: patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software. Crucially, the territoriality rules distinguish between professional preparation services and official government filing fees: supporting activities such as prior-art searches, patent drafting, and application preparation would be eligible only if conducted in Canada, whereas official foreign patent office filing and maintenance fees would qualify even when remitted to foreign IP authorities. Costs related to IP enforcement, infringement litigation, or commercial licensing negotiations would be excluded. Furthermore, to prevent tax-subsidized IP stripping, if a taxpayer subsequently disposes of IP whose registration or maintenance costs generated SR&ED tax incentives, statutory recapture rules would apply to claw back the associated SR&ED deduction and ITC.
2.4 Complementary Federal Innovation Measures

Alongside the direct amendments to Sections 37 and 127 of the ITA, the federal government introduced parallel fiscal and grant instruments during the 2024–2026 cycle that interact directly with corporate R&D tax planning. Under Budget 2024 and the August 12, 2024 legislative proposals, businesses were granted an Accelerated Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) for productivity-enhancing assets, permitting an immediate 100% first-year write-off of the cost of patents, data network infrastructure equipment, computers, and other general-purpose electronic data processing equipment acquired on or after April 16, 2024, and available for use before January 1, 2027. Taxpayers acquiring dual-use computing infrastructure must strategically evaluate whether to claim the asset under the restored SR&ED capital expenditure regime (Line 390 or Line 504 of Form T661) or under Schedule T2SCH8 Accelerated CCA, as subsection 37(1) and CRA guidelines strictly prohibit double-claiming the same capital cost across Form T661 and Schedule 8.

In parallel, Budget 2024 allocated $2.4 billion to Canada's artificial intelligence ecosystem, comprising $2 billion for the AI Compute Access Fund and Canadian AI Sovereign Compute Strategy, $200 million to accelerate sectoral AI adoption through regional development agencies, $100 million for the National Research Council's (NRC) Industrial Research Assistance Program (IRAP) AI Assist Program supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), and $50 million for workforce transition, alongside establishing the AI Safety Institute of Canada. Because direct cost-shared grants from NRC IRAP or the $2-billion Global Innovation Clusters constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, recipients must deduct such funding dollar-for-dollar from their qualified SR&ED expenditure pools.

Finally, following public consultations that closed on April 15, 2024, regarding the creation of a preferential federal patent box regime, the federal government maintained the general federal corporate income tax rate at 15.0% (and 15.0% for manufacturing and processing profits), with the federal small business tax rate fixed at 9.0% on the first $500,000 of active business income, while providing $14.5 million over two years to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's (ISED) Innovation Asset Collective. Concurrently, Canada enacted the Global Minimum Tax Act implementing OECD Pillar Two, which imposes a 15% minimum effective tax rate on large multinational enterprise groups. Under Pillar Two rules, refundable tax credits meeting Qualified Refundable Tax Credit (QRTC) criteria—such as refundable SR&ED ITCs—are treated more favourably as income in the effective tax rate denominator rather than a direct reduction of covered taxes in the numerator, preserving the value of refundable Canadian R&D incentives for in-scope multinationals.

body.text: 3. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures and Overhead Calculation Methodologies

To generate an SR&ED deduction under subsection 37(1) and an ITC under subsection 127(9), an expenditure must be directly attributable to the prosecution of eligible SR&ED work in Canada. Claimants must elect annually, on a business-by-business basis when filing Form T661, between two mutually exclusive accounting methodologies for capturing SR&ED overhead: the Traditional Method or the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method. Once elected for a taxation year, the choice is irrevocable for that year.
3.1 Direct Labour, Specified Employees, and Remuneration Exclusions

Across both the Traditional and Proxy methods, employee salaries and wages constitute the foundational cost driver of Canadian SR&ED claims. Eligibility is governed strictly by the nature of the technical duties performed by the individual rather than job title or academic credentials. Claimable personnel consist of employees directly engaged in hands-on basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work, extending to first-line technical supervisors to the extent their supervision directly guides the technical execution of the experimental investigation. Administrative, executive, legal, and human resources personnel are excluded from direct labour, though a portion of their remuneration may be captured under the Traditional Method if directly incremental to SR&ED, or implicitly covered via the 55% PPA. Where Canadian-resident employees perform permissible SR&ED support work outside Canada, foreign salaries are capped at 10% of the total eligible SR&ED salaries and wages paid for work performed in Canada.

The Income Tax Act and Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations impose rigorous anti-avoidance constraints on owner-managers through the concept of a "specified employee"—defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who is a specified shareholder (owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or any related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer. Under subsections 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9) of the ITR, specified employees are subject to strict remuneration ceilings designed to prevent corporations from distributing corporate profits as tax-subsidized R&D wages. First, whereas arm's-length (non-specified) employees may have bonuses and profit-based remuneration included in direct SR&ED wages (though excluded from the PPA salary base), specified employees are completely barred from claiming bonuses or remuneration based on profits as SR&ED expenditures. Second, the maximum direct salary or wages claimable for a specified employee is capped at five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee, and shared across all associated corporations employing that individual. Third, under subsection 2900(7) of the ITR, when computing the salary base for the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), the maximum eligible salary of a specified employee is further restricted to the lesser of 75% of the employee's total salary and wages (less exclusions) and 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated for the days employed as a specified employee.

Furthermore, for all employees (both specified and non-specified), subsection 2900(9) of the ITR mandates four universal exclusions from the PPA salary base: taxable benefits under sections 6 and 7 (including employee stock option benefits under section 7); unpaid remuneration from a prior taxation year that is paid in the current year and deemed incurred under subsection 78(4) (reported separately on Line 310 of Form T661); remuneration based on profits; and bonuses. Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, any salary or wages accrued at year-end that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are denied in the year of accrual and may only be claimed on Line 310 in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid.
3.2 Traditional Method vs. Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method

Under the Traditional Method, a claimant must identify, track, and substantiate every individual overhead and other expenditure that is directly attributable and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada pursuant to subsection 2900(2) of the ITR, reporting these itemized costs on Line 360 of Form T661. Additionally, under the Traditional Method, only the exact proportion of an employee's time directly engaged in hands-on SR&ED may be claimed.

Conversely, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method—governed by subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) to (VI) of the ITA and subsections 2900(4) through 2900(10) of the ITR—eliminates the administrative burden of tracking itemized SR&ED overhead costs by substituting a notional statutory formula calculated in Part 5 of Form T661. Since the 2014 taxation year, subsection 2900(4) of the ITR fixes the PPA rate at 55% of the claimant's eligible SR&ED salary base, following its phased reduction from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013.

Two nuanced statutory mechanics govern the PPA method in practice. First, under subsection 2900(5) of the ITR, the "all or substantially all" (ASA) labour rule stipulates that if an arm's-length employee spends 90% or more of their working time in the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of that employee's eligible salary or wages counts toward the SR&ED claim and the PPA salary base. Second, the PPA is a notional figure that exists solely inside the definition of "qualified expenditure" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA to generate SR&ED ITCs. The PPA itself is never added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool; instead, the actual underlying overhead expenses (such as shop supplies, utilities, and clerical support staff) are deducted by the taxpayer as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1) of the ITA. To prevent a taxpayer from claiming a notional PPA that exceeds its total actual business overhead, subsection 2900(6) of the ITR imposes an overall cap on the PPA computed via the statutory formula:
PPA cap = A − B − C

In this formula, A represents the total of all amounts deducted in computing the taxpayer's net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold), while B and C subtract specific non-overhead deductions (B: deductions claimed under sections 20, 24, 26, 30, 32, 37, 66 to 66.8 and 104 of the ITA, such as capital cost allowance, interest, bad debts and SR&ED expenditures deducted under Section 37; C: expenditures for the use of, or the right to use, a building) to isolate the maximum permissible overhead ceiling.
3.3 Materials, Subcontractors, and Third-Party Payments

Beyond direct labour and overhead, claimants may include the cost of materials that are either consumed (rendered virtually valueless or destroyed during experimentation) or transformed (incorporated into an experimental prototype or pilot plant during systematic testing) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. If an experimental prototype or pilot batch is subsequently sold commercially or converted to commercial use during a production run, the CRA's SR&ED During Production Runs Policy and statutory recapture rules require the lesser of the fair market value or proceeds of disposition and the original claimed material cost to be clawed back from the SR&ED expenditure pool.

Where a claimant contracts out eligible SR&ED work to an arm's-length contractor that performs the work in Canada, 100% of the contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deduction pool, but subsection 127(9) restricts the "qualified expenditure" for ITC purposes to 80% of the eligible contract payment—a statutory 20% haircut designed to strip out the contractor's assumed profit margin. If the subcontractor does not deal at arm's length with the claimant, the 80% rule does not apply; instead, the claim is restricted to the non-arm's-length performer's actual qualified SR&ED costs, and no PPA is generated on subcontracted labour. Similarly, payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit SR&ED corporations for SR&ED performed in Canada to which the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results are reported on Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) and are likewise subject to the 80% inclusion rule for ITC purposes.
3.4 Capital Property, Lease Costs, and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE)

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (and for property acquired or lease payments first becoming payable after December 15, 2024), the CRA's updated Form T661 architecture governs capital and lease claims through strict operational thresholds. An SR&ED capital expenditure is defined as an expenditure made to acquire new or used depreciable property after December 15, 2024, that the claimant intends either to use all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to consume ASA (90% or more) of its value to perform SR&ED in Canada. Land (a non-depreciable asset), buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are statutorily ineligible. Expenditures for qualifying new or used equipment meeting the 90% ASA test are entered on Line 390 of Form T661 and must be excluded from Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance). If the equipment is later sold or converted to commercial use, Line 440 triggers SR&ED CCA recapture. Where capital expenditures are transferred between non-arm's-length parties, the transferor and transferee report the qualifying post-December 15, 2024 amounts on Lines 535 and 540 of Form T661.

When a taxpayer acquires new equipment after December 15, 2024, that is used partially for SR&ED and partially for commercial operations—thereby failing the 90% ASA test—the asset may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 of Form T661, provided it is not prescribed depreciable property (PDP) and is used for both SR&ED and non-SR&ED purposes across two statutory evaluation periods known as the "first term" and the "second term". While the capital cost of SUE does not enter the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (instead, normal CCA is claimed on Schedule 8), SUE generates a partial SR&ED ITC across the first term and second term under both the Traditional and Proxy methods.

With respect to leased assets, lease payments first becoming payable after December 15, 2024, for equipment used ASA (90% or more) in SR&ED qualify under both the Traditional and Proxy methods. If equipment is used less than 90% of its operating time in SR&ED, its lease costs are completely excluded under the Proxy method (as they are subsumed by the 55% PPA), but may be claimed proportionally on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures if the taxpayer elects the Traditional Method.

body.text: 4. Sub-National R&D Tax Credit Regimes: Provincial and Territorial Integration

Canadian corporations performing R&D benefit from a two-tier fiscal architecture in which provincial and territorial governments supplement the federal SR&ED ITC with jurisdiction-specific R&D tax credits. With the exception of Quebec and Alberta—which maintain independent provincial tax administration for their corporate R&D incentives through Revenu Québec and Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration, respectively—provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the CRA through harmonized schedules attached to the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return.
4.1 Quebec: The 2025 Consolidation into the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

In the Quebec Provincial Budget tabled on March 25, 2025 (detailed in Quebec Ministry of Finance Information Bulletin 2025-6), the Government of Quebec executed a sweeping structural transformation of its R&D tax architecture. For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec abolished eight separate legacy R&D and innovation tax measures—most notably the long-standing Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) previously claimed on Form RD-1029.7 (which offered a 14% base rate and up to 30% for SMEs)—and consolidated them into a single, flagship refundable incentive: the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), supported by a $2.4 billion five-year fiscal allocation.

The CRIC regime introduces fundamental structural shifts for corporations operating a business and maintaining an establishment in Quebec. Unlike federal SR&ED or Quebec's repealed RD-1029.7 credit—which tied enhanced rates to corporate size or global assets—the CRIC applies an identical, 100% refundable two-tier rate schedule to all eligible corporations (whether startups, SMEs, or large multinationals), while excluding individuals, trusts, and certain public corporations. Specifically, an eligible corporation receives a 30% refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures that exceed the applicable annual exclusion threshold, and a 20% refundable tax credit on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 band.

Before any expenditure generates a CRIC benefit, a corporation's annual qualified expenditures must surpass a statutory exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations). The exclusion threshold equals the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Quebec personal income tax Basic Personal Amount ($18,571 in 2025) for each employee claiming eligible time, adjusted proportionally for the exact percentage of working time that employee devoted to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities during the taxation year. While Quebec remains fully harmonized with subsection 248(1) of the federal ITA for core R&D definitions (and relies on the CRA to conduct the scientific review of R&D work), the CRIC expands provincial eligibility beyond pure R&D to encompass pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Quebec in conjunction with R&D work carried out in Quebec by the corporation or on its behalf. Eligible pre-commercialization work specifically covers tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to satisfy regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation, as well as product design work, including the development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, packaging design, and choice of materials.

Under the CRIC, qualified expenditures incurred in Quebec encompass four cost categories: 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for eligible R&D or pre-commercialization work in Quebec; 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors for eligible contracts executed in Quebec; 50% of payments made to an eligible Quebec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity; and 100% of property acquisition costs for new depreciable capital equipment acquired to perform R&D or pre-commercialization in Quebec. Costs relating to the acquisition of land, buildings, or a right to use land or buildings are excluded, as is any property used or acquired to be used as part of a Large Investment Project tax holiday qualification certificate. Unlike federal SR&ED, the CRIC does not provide a proxy overhead allowance, and the same capital asset cannot be double-claimed under both the CRIC and Quebec's C3i Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation. To claim the CRIC, an eligible corporation must complete Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (and Form RD-1029.8.CR) and attach it to its Quebec corporate income tax return.
4.2 Ontario: OITC, OBRITC, and ORDTC

Corporations maintaining a permanent establishment in Ontario can stack three distinct provincial SR&ED tax credits, each administered by the CRA and harmonized with federal eligibility determinations. The primary small-business incentive is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), administered by the CRA for taxation years ending after December 31, 2008, and claimed on Schedule 566 (T2SCH566) attached to Form T661 and the T2 return without a separate provincial application. The OITC provides a refundable tax credit on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures for eligible corporations, operating alongside the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) for qualifying research contracts with eligible Ontario post-secondary institutions and hospital research institutes, and the non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC).
4.3 Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Following the expiration of the legacy Alberta SR&ED tax credit, the Government of Alberta enacted the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) for qualifying R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020. Delivered directly through the Alberta corporate income tax system without a separate grant pre-application and administered pursuant to Information Circular IEG-1, the IEG is claimed by filing AT1 Schedule 29 and AT1 Schedule 29 Listing alongside the Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (AT1).

The IEG utilizes a two-tier incremental formula designed to reward year-over-year R&D expansion in Alberta on up to a $4,000,000 annual expenditure cap that must be allocated among associated corporations. Qualified corporations receive an 8% base refundable payment on eligible R&D spending carried out in Alberta up to the corporation's "base level of spending," which is calculated as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the immediately preceding two taxation years. For eligible R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's two-year average base spending level, the corporation earns an enhanced 20% refundable payment up to the $4 million annual expenditure cap. Consequently, a startup or corporation conducting R&D in Alberta for the first time with a zero-dollar two-year historical base earns the full 20% refundable rate on its entire eligible spend up to $4 million.

To ensure fiscal support targets small and medium-sized companies, the $4 million IEG expenditure limit phases out incrementally for corporations (and associated groups) with between $10 million and $50 million in taxable capital, and firms with $50 million or more in taxable capital are completely ineligible for the grant. Eligible IEG expenditures strictly match those that qualify for the federal SR&ED program under Form T661, provided they are incurred in Alberta.

body.text: 4.4 Mathematical Mechanics of Federal-Provincial Government Assistance Stacking

Pursuant to subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the federal ITA—and as detailed in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy—all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (as well as direct grants such as NRC IRAP) constitute "government assistance". Consequently, federal and provincial tax credit rates cannot simply be added together; rather, the provincial credit reduces the federal qualified expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar before the federal SR&ED ITC is computed:
Federal SR&ED ITC = (qualified SR&ED expenditures − provincial R&D tax credits and other government assistance) × federal ITC rate

To illustrate this interaction in Quebec under the post-March 25, 2025 CRIC regime, consider a practical corporate scenario where a Quebec enterprise incurs $1,000,000 in eligible innovation expenditures ($800,000 in R&D salaries paid to eight employees working full time on eligible activities, $100,000 in new lab equipment, and $100,000 in university research contracts, of which 50% or $50,000 is eligible for CRIC, yielding $950,000 in gross eligible CRIC spend). The exclusion threshold is the greater of $50,000 and 8 × $18,571 = $148,568, so $801,432 of qualified expenditures exceeds the threshold; because this amount falls entirely within the first $1,000,000 band, the corporation earns a 30% refundable CRIC of approximately $240,430. Because the Quebec CRIC is government assistance, it reduces the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool prior to applying the 35% federal CCPC rate (or 15% base rate), generating combined federal-provincial effective tax recovery rates that routinely approach or exceed 50% of total qualifying R&D outlays. Furthermore, any government assistance or federal ITC claimed reduces deductible expenses or is included in taxable income in the subsequent taxation year, requiring coordinated multi-year tax modelling.
5. Administrative Governance, Filing Compliance, and Audit Defence Protocols
5.1 The CRA's 2021 Eligibility Guidelines: The "Why" and "How" Framework

In August 2021, the CRA archived its 2015 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (as well as legacy sector-specific documents such as the December 2012 software development application guidance) and promulgated the consolidated Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives. While the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) of the ITA remained unchanged, the 2021 Guidelines reorganized the CRA's administrative review methodology from the historical five-question checklist into a streamlined two-pillar inquiry known as the "Why" and "How" Requirements.

The first pillar—the "Why" Requirement—examines the underlying scientific or technological purpose of the project by asking why the work was conducted. The claimant must establish that the work was undertaken for the purpose of generating new scientific or technological knowledge—achieving a scientific or technological advancement—because the project encountered a scientific or technological uncertainty that could not be resolved using standard practice, publicly available knowledge, or routine engineering. The 2021 Guidelines draw a sharp demarcation between an eligible technological uncertainty and an ineligible technical problem. A technical problem may be highly complex, expensive, or novel to the company, but if its resolution can be deduced from existing engineering principles or resolved by adopting a known workaround rather than investigating the underlying technological limitation, the work fails the "Why" test. Conversely, system uncertainty—arising when integrating known components that interact unpredictably and require modifying the underlying subsystem technologies—satisfies the "Why" requirement, whereas mere doubt about commercial success or cost targets never constitutes technological uncertainty.

The second pillar—the "How" Requirement—evaluates the methodology of the project by asking how the work was conducted, consolidating the last four legacy SR&ED eligibility questions. The claimant must demonstrate that the scientific or technological uncertainty was investigated through a structured, systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Under the 2021 Guidelines, fulfilling the "How" requirement necessitates four sequential building blocks: setting clear objectives and measurable indicators early in the investigation; formulating a specific hypothesis—an idea consistent with known facts set up to be proved or disproved—aimed at reducing or eliminating the uncertainty; testing the hypothesis through a planned experiment or analysis; and drawing logical conclusions from the results while keeping contemporaneous records as the work progresses. Working systematically according to a commercial project plan or engaging in unstructured trial-and-error—trying options until one works without formulating causal hypotheses—is insufficient on its own to satisfy the "How" requirement.
5.2 Mandatory Filing Forms, Statutory Deadlines, and Processing Standards

To perfect a legal claim for SR&ED deductions and ITCs, a corporate taxpayer must submit a prescribed package of tax schedules with its T2 Corporation Income Tax Return. The core submission is Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), which captures project-by-project technical narratives, expenditure tabulations, qualified expenditure calculations, Part 5 Prescribed Proxy Amount computations, and claim statistics. Line-by-line instructions for completing Form T661 are published in CRA Guide T4088 (Guide to Form T661). Alongside Form T661, corporations must file Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) to claim, carry forward, carry back, or transfer their SR&ED ITCs, and Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) whenever claiming payments made to third-party universities or research institutes.

Under the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, a taxpayer's statutory filing deadline depends on its tax filing category, falling between 15 and 18 months from the end of the fiscal year in which the expenditures were incurred. Specifically, corporate tax filers have an absolute statutory deadline of 18 months from the end of the taxation year to submit Form T661 and Schedule 31. The CRA cannot legally extend this 18-month statutory bar unless the deadline falls on a weekend or public holiday, in which case it shifts to the next business day. Consequently, authoritative compliance practice dictates filing the SR&ED claim within 6 months of the corporate year-end alongside the initial T2 return, preserving a full 12-month window to file technical or financial amendments before the 18-month deadline expires. Once submitted, the CRA processes refundable claims accepted without review within 60 calendar days of filing, refundable claims selected for audit review within 180 calendar days, and non-refundable claims within 365 calendar days, assuming the claimant responds promptly to CRA document requests.
5.3 Pre-Claim Advisory Services and Contemporaneous Documentation Standards

To address the information gap faced by potential and new claimants, the CRA provides a suite of free advisory and diagnostic services. Claimants can begin with the Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT), a confidential online and downloadable two-step diagnostic tool that helps businesses evaluate whether their work meets the "Why" and "How" tests and estimates expected SR&ED tax credits without saving or transmitting any data to the CRA. Prior to filing a claim, Canadian-based businesses can request a Pre-Claim Consultation (PCC) or a Pre-Claim Review (PCR)—services that replaced the legacy Pre-Claim Project Review (PCPR)—to obtain upfront CRA feedback or a written eligibility report on in-progress or completed R&D projects, provided the work has not already received an eligibility determination and is not under Notice of Objection or litigation. For first-time claimants who have already submitted a claim, the CRA operates the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS), a half-day educational session conducted by local CRA officials to advise the business on identifying eligible work, tracking allowable expenditures, and maintaining compliant documentation for future claims, complemented by the Account Executive (AE) and Liaison Officer services.

If an SR&ED claim is selected for audit review, CRA technical and financial reviewers require contemporaneous supporting evidence generated as the SR&ED work was being carried out. In accordance with CRA Guide RC4409 (Keeping Records) and Information Circular IC78-10R5 (Books and Records Retention/Destruction), acceptable evidence includes project planning documents, dated design specifications, hypothesis and testing logs, photographs, physical samples, time sheets, payroll reconciliations, general ledgers, contracts, and invoices. Claimants remain legally responsible for the accuracy and compliance of their signed SR&ED applications even if misled by third-party promotions, and preparers and planners are subject to third-party civil penalties under Information Circular IC01-1.
6. Dispute Resolution, Notices of Objection, and Foundational Jurisprudence
6.1 Statutory Dispute Resolution: Notices of Objection and Tax Court Appeals

When a taxpayer disagrees with a Notice of Assessment, Notice of Reassessment, or Notice of Determination reducing or denying an SR&ED claim, the formal dispute resolution architecture under subsections 165(1) and 169(1) of the ITA governs the appellate trajectory. At the first stage, a corporate taxpayer must serve a written Notice of Objection on the Minister of National Revenue (electronically via the CRA online account or by mail to the Chief of Appeals, Appeals Intake Centre, 1050 Notre Dame Avenue) on or before the day that is 90 days after the day of sending of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment. For individuals (other than trusts) and graduated rate estates, the deadline is the later of 90 days after the day of sending of the notice or one year after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year. Crucially, the 90-day countdown clock starts on the date the Notice of Assessment is printed and mailed by the CRA, not the date the taxpayer receives it.

Two procedural traps frequently arise at the objection stage. First, no valid Notice of Objection can be filed in respect of a "nil assessment"—a situation where a reassessment reduces carryforward pools or losses but results in no taxes, penalties, or interest being payable for the year. Second, under the Notice of Objection standards for large corporations, every disputed issue must be explicitly pleaded in the objection; otherwise, subsection 169(2.1) of the ITA bars the taxpayer from appealing the omitted issue to the Tax Court of Canada.

If the 90-day objection deadline is missed, the taxpayer may apply to the Minister for an extension of time under section 166.1 of the ITA. Pursuant to subsection 166.1(7), the Minister can grant an extension only if the application is made within one year after the expiration of the initial 90-day deadline (within 1 year and 90 days of the sending of the assessment) and the taxpayer demonstrates that within the 90-day window it was unable to act or had a bona fide intention to object, that it would be just and equitable to grant the extension, and that the application was made as soon as circumstances permitted. If the Minister refuses the extension request, the taxpayer has 90 days from the mailing of the refusal notification to apply to the Tax Court of Canada under section 166.2. As detailed in Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC (2024-842), when a taxpayer asserts that a Notice of Assessment was never mailed, the Court applies a four-step framework utilizing CRA officer affidavits under subsection 244(14) of the ITA to verify mailing records.

Upon receipt of a valid Notice of Objection, subsection 165(3) obligates the Minister (through an independent Appeals Officer) to reconsider the assessment and vacate, confirm, or vary it, or reassess, and notify the taxpayer in writing. Under subsection 169(1) of the ITA, once the Minister confirms the assessment or reassesses—or if 90 days have elapsed after serving the Notice of Objection without a response from the Minister—the taxpayer may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada (under the Informal Procedure or General Procedure), provided the appeal is filed no later than 90 days after the confirmation or reassessment is mailed. Missing that 90-day statutory window generally terminates the dispute.
6.2 Canonical and Contemporary SR&ED Jurisprudence

Canadian judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1) of the ITA is anchored by a binding line of Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) decisions that govern how technical eligibility and evidentiary burdens are adjudicated. The foundational authority in Canadian law is Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839. At paragraph 16 of Northwest Hydraulic, the Tax Court articulated the five-question legal test for determining whether claimed work constitutes SR&ED: first, whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or habitual procedures; second, whether the person claiming SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; third, whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including formulating, testing, and modifying the hypotheses; fourth, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement (an advancement in general understanding, even if the prototype failed commercially); and fifth, whether the taxpayer kept a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed.

In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393 (affirming 2000 DTC 2372), the Federal Court of Appeal formally adopted the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as binding appellate law across Canada. Subsequent Tax Court jurisprudence has consistently applied these criteria to distinguish eligible experimental development from skilled commercial engineering. In Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65, and Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (at paragraph 33), the Tax Court held that complex software development and custom mechanical rigging fail to qualify as SR&ED where the taxpayer relies on routine engineering or trial-and-error adjustments rather than conducting a systematic investigation grounded in explicit hypothesis testing.

Following the CRA's August 2021 revision of its administrative guidelines, taxpayers challenged whether the five-part test remained mandatory. In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, the Federal Court of Appeal had already rejected the argument that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria do not apply because the statutory definition does not refer to the scientific method, and in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (affirming 2020 TCC 47), it definitively resolved this question. In National R&D Inc., the taxpayer appealed the denial of software SR&ED credits, arguing that the CRA's 2021 Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives had removed the requirement to follow the scientific method. Dismissing the appeal, the FCA echoed Kam-Press in holding that it is the role of the courts—not CRA administrative guidelines—to interpret and elaborate on the meaning of ITA provisions, and confirmed that the 2021 CRA guidelines did not remove the requirement to follow the scientific method under Northwest Hydraulic. The FCA also affirmed the exclusion of the taxpayer's expert witness report because the expert improperly opined on the ultimate legal issue of whether the work constituted SR&ED. Most recently, in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2024 TCC 159 (Informal Procedure), the Tax Court applied the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria and allowed the taxpayer's appeal, finding that a project to develop a shelf-stable, canned, cold-pressed beverage satisfied all five criteria, and in Tuna Temple Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2026 FCA 175 (affirming 2025 TCC 183), the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the taxpayer's appeal, confirming that the Tax Court had correctly identified the five criteria and that the taxpayer bears the onus of refuting the Minister's assumptions; both decisions confirm that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria and contemporaneous experimental record-keeping remain the decisive legal standard across all Canadian industries.

body.text: 7. Strategic Synthesis and Compliance Recommendations for Corporate Claimants

The legislative and judicial trajectory of Canada's R&D tax ecosystem between 2024 and 2026 reflects a deliberate policy divergence between statutory expansion of the expenditure base and judicial tightening of evidentiary rigour. On the legislative front, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, the March 2025 Quebec CRIC consolidation, and the Budget 2026 proposals have substantially expanded, or propose to expand, the financial generosity and commercial reach of Canadian R&D incentives—raising the federal 35% expenditure limit, opening refundable credits to Canadian public corporations, restoring capital equipment eligibility, and integrating regulatory validation testing, product design (in Quebec), and IP registration costs into the claimable tax base. Simultaneously, however, the Federal Court of Appeal and Tax Court of Canada in National R&D Inc. (2022 FCA 72), Manning Canning (2024 TCC 159), and Tuna Temple (2026 FCA 175) have continued to apply the Northwest Hydraulic criteria and made clear that administrative simplifications in CRA guidance do not relax the taxpayer's legal burden to prove strict adherence to the scientific method and contemporaneous record-keeping under Northwest Hydraulic.

To optimize tax recovery while insulating claims against CRA reassessment, corporate claimants and tax auditors must implement disciplined operational controls across four interconnected domains. First, with the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures after December 15, 2024, the launch of Quebec's CRIC for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, and the proposed Budget 2026 expansion to regulatory certification testing and IP registration costs, enterprises should configure their accounting systems to tag capital equipment operating time (substantiating the 90% ASA test on Line 390 versus SUE on Line 504), regulatory testing invoices, and domestic versus foreign patent prosecution fees directly to specific, eligible SR&ED project codes. Second, corporations operating in Quebec must model the interplay between the 30% and 20% refundable CRIC (which covers pre-commercialization, 50% of subcontractors, and capital property without a proxy overhead allowance) and the federal SR&ED regime (which provides a 55% PPA on direct wages), ensuring capital assets are allocated optimally between the CRIC, Quebec's C3i credit, and federal Accelerated CCA (Schedule 8) versus Form T661 Line 390 without violating anti-double-claiming rules. Third, engineering and software teams must capture the five Northwest Hydraulic elements—and the CRA's 2021 "Why" and "How" building blocks—contemporaneously within their project management and laboratory logs as the work progresses, explicitly recording why existing knowledge failed, the specific hypothesis formulated, the experimental protocol executed, and the quantitative results observed. Finally, corporate tax departments must enforce strict calendar controls to file Form T661 and Schedule 31 within 6 months of fiscal year-end alongside the original T2 return—well ahead of the unforgiving 18-month statutory bar—and immediately calendar the 90-day deadline from the printing and mailing date of any Notice of Assessment or Reassessment to preserve objection rights under subsection 165(1).
